title: Component-Based Decomposition Patterns
subtitle: Turn recognizable code boundaries into domain services
summary: Component-based decomposition is an incremental path from a monolith toward separately deployed domain services. The chapter presents a sequence of patterns that makes the work observable and controllable. First identify and size components, using code metrics and fitness functions to expose oversized or unstable areas. Gather common domain components, distinguishing business functionality shared by some workflows from infrastructure shared by all. Flatten components when nested structure hides the true boundary. Determine component dependencies to reveal direction, cycles, and extraction order. Create component domains by grouping related components around a business capability, then create domain services as deployable units. The Sysops Squad reporting example turns one oversized component into shared, ticket, expert, and financial reporting components. The patterns preserve incremental refactoring, but shared code, dependency direction, and deployment boundaries still demand explicit trade-off analysis.

concepts.title: Identify and size
concepts.body: Begin by inventorying logical components and measuring their relative size rather than guessing from names. The Sysops Squad analysis finds Reporting at roughly one third of the codebase, making it a candidate for refinement. Size is a signal for investigation, not a universal threshold; architects combine it with cohesion, coupling, and the business change that the boundary must support.
concepts.example: Teaching extension: split a large Reporting component into shared utilities plus ticket, expert, and financial reporting areas after confirming their responsibilities.

concepts.title: Gather common domain
concepts.body: Common domain functionality is business processing reused by some workflows, such as notification, validation, or formatting. It differs from common infrastructure such as logging, metrics, and security. Gathering common domain behavior can remove duplication and clarify ownership, but a shared component can also become a new coupling hub if its scope is too broad.
concepts.example: Teaching extension: consolidate customer, ticket, and survey notification behavior into a Notification component with an explicit domain responsibility.

concepts.title: Flatten components
concepts.body: Nested components can obscure the architecture’s actual boundaries. Flattening makes the logical component list and dependencies easier to inspect, which supports later grouping and extraction. The pattern is a structural clarification step: it does not by itself define a service boundary or remove every dependency.
concepts.example: Teaching extension: flatten a reporting package tree so the team can see shared queries beside each report family and decide which belong together.

concepts.title: Determine dependencies
concepts.body: After components are visible, map the direction and strength of their dependencies. This exposes cycles and shared assets that complicate extraction, and it informs a safe sequence for refactoring. Dependency analysis turns an architectural diagram into a working migration plan, with fitness functions able to prevent new cycles while the code changes.
concepts.example: Teaching extension: identify that Expert Reports depends on shared report formatting while Financial Reports also reaches billing code, then isolate those contracts before extraction.

concepts.title: Create component domains
concepts.body: Component domains group related components around a coherent business capability. The grouping should follow functional cohesion and change drivers, rather than convenient package proximity. A domain boundary gives teams a candidate unit for ownership and later deployment, while dependency evidence tests whether the grouping is viable.
concepts.example: Teaching extension: group Ticket, Ticket Assign, Ticket Notify, and Ticket Route into a Ticketing domain after checking their shared data and communication contracts.

concepts.title: Create domain services
concepts.body: The final pattern turns component domains into separately deployed domain services. This is an incremental move toward a service-based architecture: the service boundary follows the refined domain rather than an arbitrary technical layer. Deployment separation adds operational work, so teams must carry forward dependency governance, contracts, and the limits of shared data.
concepts.example: Teaching extension: deploy Ticketing and Reporting as separate units while retaining a controlled transition around the existing database, then tackle data separation as a later decision.

misconceptions.claim: Every shared function should become a shared service immediately.
misconceptions.correction: Shared domain behavior and shared infrastructure have different roles; broad sharing can create a coupling hub and should be evaluated against ownership and change.
Deployment boundaries are only one step; dependencies, contracts, data ownership, and governance still determine whether the architecture is healthy.

scenario.title: Refine reporting
scenario.context: Reporting accounts for a large part of a monolith and includes common formatters, queries, and distribution logic alongside ticket, expert, and financial reports. The team can create a shared reporting component first, or immediately deploy three independent report services.

options.label: Refine then group
options.benefit: Makes responsibilities and dependencies visible before choosing deployable domains.
options.cost: Delays independent deployment while refactoring and measuring the components.
options.consequence: The team separates shared domain logic, maps dependencies, groups report families, and then deploys boundaries supported by evidence.

options.label: Deploy immediately
options.benefit: May isolate report load quickly and provide an early operational boundary.
options.cost: Unexamined shared queries and formatters can become cross-service coupling or duplicated logic.
options.consequence: Three services launch, but a common change requires coordinated releases; the team later refactors the boundaries under production pressure.

scenario.debrief: The patterns are a sequence of discovery and refinement. Speed can matter, but a visible dependency map and coherent domain grouping reduce the chance of distributing the monolith’s existing tangles.

quiz.question: What did the Sysops Squad sizing exercise reveal?
options: Reporting was a significant oversized component
quiz.explanation: The reporting component’s large share justified breaking it into coherent reporting areas.

quiz.question: How does common domain functionality differ from infrastructure?
options: Domain logic serves business processing; infrastructure is broadly operational
quiz.explanation: The distinction guides ownership and prevents treating all reuse as the same kind of dependency.

quiz.question: Why determine component dependencies before creating services?
options: To reveal cycles and extraction constraints
quiz.explanation: Dependency direction and shared assets determine viable grouping and migration order.

exercise.title: Apply the pattern sequence
exercise.prompt: Take one monolithic area and walk it through sizing, common-domain review, flattening, dependency mapping, domain grouping, and a proposed service boundary.

steps.text: Measure candidate components and find oversized or risky areas.
Gather common domain behavior and flatten hidden nesting.
Map dependency direction, shared assets, and cycles.
Group cohesive components around a business capability.
Choose a deployable domain boundary and govern its contracts.
